chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abd Allah, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:
I said to him: I feel wind in my belly until I think that it has come out. So he said, “There is no wudu (ablution) upon you until you hear the sound or find the wind.”
Then he said, “Indeed, Iblis comes and sits between the buttocks of a man and breaks wind in order to make him doubt.”

key_terms.إِبْلِيسَ: Iblis, who seeks to cast doubt and misgivings into a person
key_terms.الرِّيحَ: wind, meaning passing gas that would invalidate wudu when certain
key_terms.الصَّوْتَ: the sound by which certainty of passing wind is established
key_terms.لِيُشَكِّكَهُ: to cause him doubt or uncertainty regarding his state of purity
key_terms.وُضُوءٌ: wudu (ablution), the state or act of ritual purification for worship

ai.seo_question: Does feeling movement in the stomach invalidate wudu (ablution) if one is not certain that wind came out?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling concerning doubt in ritual purity and wudu (ablution). It establishes that wudu is not invalidated by mere suspicion, but only by certainty such as hearing a sound or perceiving the wind, and it warns that such doubts may be from Iblis.
